paragraphs.text: “The actual significance of the word sáhitya [loosely, ‘literature’] is inherent in the word itself. Sáhitya is defined as that whose characteristic is to move with (sahita = “with”) the trends of life… The word sáhitya can be interpreted in another way as well: sa + hita = hitena saha, “that which co-exists with hita [welfare]”. Where there is no inner spirit of welfare, we cannot use the term sáhitya. The creations or compositions of those who proclaim, “Art for artʼs sake,” cannot be treated as sáhitya… Thus literature is that which moves together with society and leads society towards true fulfilment and welfare by providing the inspiration to serve. The statement “Art for artʼs sake” is not acceptable; rather we should say, “Art for service and blessedness.”… Those who are inferior and neglected, helpless and destitute – whom society considers to be infernal maggots – are the very people who are the most unrepresented in the salons of literature… The sáhityika or the artist has to take the responsibility of enabling them to rise up and sit in the same row with the rest of society, after dusting off the dirt from their bodies…

paragraphs.text: Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar (also known as Shrii Shrii Ánandamúrti, a spiritual Guru) elaborately explained his views on art and literature in the discourse (“The Practice of Art and Literature”, A Few Problems Solved Part 1) quoted from above. But he did not stop there. Advancing further, he translated his words into actions, creating a direct example in the form of his own literature, marked by his natural ease and aptitude. Thus we get a great series named Sarkarʼs Short Stories in fourteen parts. In June 1985, the first Bengali fourteen-part set was published under the authorʼs direct guidance. In January 1990, the English Sarkarʼs Short Stories Part 1 was published. Since then, there has been a persistent demand from our esteemed readers for the publication of all the parts. In response to that we are extremely happy to present to the readers now Sarkarʼs Short Stories Parts 1-3 in one volume. Genuine and sincere efforts are going on to publish all remaining parts within the next year. We fervently hope to fulfil this objective with the cooperation of all concerned.

paragraphs.text: All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as important and integral parts of the authorʼs writings on a vast domain of linguistics and philology which touched also on history, geography, medicine, science, art, religion, spirituality, philosophy, etc. Such books included Varńa Vijiṋána, Varńa Vicitrá (eight parts) and Shabda Cayaniká (twenty-six parts). Like most great authors, Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar is a consummate storyteller, thus he used in those books a seemingly inexhaustible supply of anecdotes, personal experiences and interesting as well as educative references, in order to capture the readerʼs interest. And it is mostly those stories that have been excerpted to constitute the present book. Thus it is natural that in the stories contained in the present book, we will find, either at the beginnings of those stories or as footnotes, relevant references to the linguistic and other subjects of the original books. In this way the stories retain the authenticity of the original books. Apart from the books mentioned above, some stories are from a volume of the authorʼs childrenʼs literature series – namely, In the Land of Hat́t́amálá.

paragraphs.text: Many readers are concerned that the authorʼs discourses, as published, should adhere as closely as possible to the precise wording the author used in speaking. For this reason, in the case of discourses given originally in English, the editors do not alter pronouns and other terms which the author in his lifetime considered “common-gender” words. As the author once said, “You know, ‘man’ is not only masculine gender, ‘man’ is common gender also. ‘Man is mortal’ – here ‘man’ means both male and female.”

paragraphs.text: Human beings look for comfort. Thus the etymological meaning of the word d́ha that we get by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root d́huńd́a, is “instrument of pleasure”; colloquially, it is called gadi [mattress or cushion]. Therefore gadi means “something which makes our lying or sitting comfortable”. The word d́ha can be used for the kind of cushion that we use under the mattress of a cot or the cushion that we use on a chair.

paragraphs.text: In North India, the word gaddá is generally used. But that does not mean that the word gaddii is not in use. However, in North and West India gaddii means “the place where the shopkeeper sits and looks after the office work or the accounts”; that is, the office. The office of various business enterprises is also called gaddii. The use of the word gaddii reminds me of the story of a merchant.

paragraphs.text: Sethjii [the merchant] was critically ill; he was on his death bed and the house was full of loud lamentation. On hearing the news of his imminent death the creditors became anxious. The debtors of Sethjii, on the other hand, had a slight glow on their faces, like the film of a thin cream of diluted milk. The children of Sethjii were terribly busy managing the matters related to the accounts of sales-tax, income-tax, excise-duty, and so on.

paragraphs.text: When Sethjii was about to breathe his last, all his seven children closed the gaddii [office] and stood by his death bed with folded hands. Sethjii started enquiring about their welfare by naming each of them. First he enquired about his eldest son. Sethjii asked, “Is Ramnajar present?” Ramnajar answered with folded hands, “Yes father, I am present”. Then he looked for the second son and asked, “Is Rampariikśań present?” Rampariikśań replied, “Yes, father, I am present.” Next he asked about the third son, “Is Ramsurath present?” Ramsurath responded, “Yes father, I am standing at your lotus feet”. Then Sethjii wanted to know about the fourth son, and asked, “Is Ramsiḿhásan present?” Ramsiḿhásan replied, “Yes father, your servant is present”. Then he enquired about the fifth son, “Is, Ramikbal present?” Ramikbal replied, “Yes father, I am standing at your feet.” Then he asked about the sixth son, “Is Rambeshan present?” Rambeshan answered, “Yes father, your servant is present”. Next he looked for the seventh son and asked, “Is Rananut́há present?” Rananut́há replied, “Your servant is here at your service.” Then the Sethjii flew into a rage and thundered, “If all seven brothers are present here then who is on the gaddii [who is looking after the office]?” As Sethjii started fuming and shouting his heart stopped and he died.

paragraphs.text: One who knows neither Hindi nor English may, on hearing Hindi, take it to be English. Also, on hearing English they may think it to be Hindi. The same kind of confusion may take place in relation to gadi and gaddii in Bengali and Hindi, respectively. When somebody says, Málik gaddii me háiṋ [The owner is in the office], a Bengali may take it to mean that the owner has been lying on the mattress of his bed. On the other hand, when a Bengali says, “Málik gadite shuye áche.” [The owner is sleeping on a mattress], someone who does not know Bengali may think that the owner is possibly lying on a bed in his shop.

paragraphs.text: Perhaps you do not know this story. Once, a rabid advocate of the national language arrived at Patna station. He was to go to the Patna secretariat but he would not use the word “secretariat” because it was English. In fact, he would not even use the word “English”. So, at the station he asked the rickshaw puller, “Please take me to the saciválay [secretariat]. The rikshaw puller was also a great lover of the national language [Hindi]! He at once retorted, “What, sáhab [sir], why are you saying saciválay, saciválay in English? Please speak in Hindi. I donʼt understand English.”

paragraphs.text: A boy of Munghyer district went to Patna to study his M. A. in Hindi. The language of his home was Auṋgiká, the language of his village was Auṋgiká and the language of his district was also Auṋgiká. The language of his umbilical cord [his mother tongue] was Auṋgiká. The language of his kitchen was Auṋgiká, the language of his house [the language of conversation of the inmates of the house] was Auṋgiká. After going to Patna, by conversing with his teachers and classmates, he had developed a good proficiency in Hindi. He also used to take part in Hindi plays. Then, during the summer holidays he came home. At noon he told his mother [in refined Hindi], “Mátah, myáṋy kśudhárta huṋ. Mujhe anna dená” [Mother, I am hungry; please give me some food].

paragraphs.text: The word d́hekur is derived from the word d́hekkar which means “to burp”. Sometimes the extravagance of intelligence is also described as d́hekure buddhi [burping intelligence]. Humans with d́hekure buddhi are intelligent but they cannot always maintain their balance. Luckily, the number of people with burping intelligence is always very small in every age and in every country. Yet, sometimes even these people with such intelligence do wonderful jobs. However, it is difficult to say whether this is due to the quality of their intelligence or just a fluke.

paragraphs.text: An oath-taking ceremony of ministers was to take place in some country of the world. It was to be held in the durbar ( 1 ) of the Governor of that place. The entire responsibility of supervising the ceremony was on the shoulders of this man with burping intelligence. The prospective ministers kept sitting with their heads tilted to one side, impatiently waiting for the auspicious moment of the oath-taking. They looked like those pots of date palm raw sugar kept on biṋd́e ( 2 ).They had donned new clothes, some had a mark of sandalwood paste on their foreheads and some had put marks of curd on their foreheads. Those who swaggered about as atheists did not put any mark on their forehead out of shyness, but hid a sanctified flower in their chest pockets and silently kept on chanting the name of their respective cherished deities, which “nobody will know about, nobody will hear.”

paragraphs.text: The greatest king of the Gupta dynasty was Samudragupta. But the name that immediately comes to the mind when we talk about the Gupta period is Chandragupta. Although Samudragupta became famous as a great conqueror, had established a huge empire in India and brought about a great change in the cultural life of the people, it was Chandragupta who was the fire brand hero of the Gupta era. His love for his subjects was legendary. It was due to his inspiration and efforts that the Sanskrit language got new life.

There are many stories about the presence of mind or the nature of the presence of mind of these ta of the theatre world. I shall tell you one or two of such stories.

When the management wanted to make a particular actor or actress or a singer popular in a short time, these people used to call out “Encore! Encore!” from different parts of the auditorium, with or without reason. In keeping harmony with them other spectators also joined them in a chorus. Everybody thought, “They must be highly talented and that is probably why we hear the applause and ‘Encore! Encore!’.” Sometime later these planted admirers used to call out, “Dádá ghurre phirre” [Brother, play it elaborately], to the tune of bala hari hari bol [“Utter the name of Hari again and again” – the chant accompanying a Hindu funeral procession]. As a result of these happenings, the name and fame of the actors and actresses used to spread far and wide.

Had he had foresight he could have envisaged that one day a powerful figure like Pramatharanjan would appear in the role of Bhima in that play. In that case he would have written some powerful dialogue for Bhiima. However, Pramatharanjan was not a person to lose heart easily. paragraphs.text: In the Bengal of those days, every educated person was familiar with the book Niiladarpańa. Dinabandhu Mitra wrote this book based on the British exploitation of the indigo planters who cultivated indigo. Although well educated, Dinabandhu Mitra used to mix with the common people and was quite familiar with their feelings and language. He was a close friend of Bankimchandra. Once he came to a village in Jessorre [a district in the former undivided Bengal, now in Bangladesh] to get an idea of the peopleʼs opinion regarding his Niiladarpańa. He was crossing the river in a boat owned by someone called Hafij Mian. From the discussion of the crew he understood that the play Niiladarpańa had been staged in their village the previous night. They were discussing only this. He asked Hafiz Mian, “Well, brother, how was the play?” He replied, “Oh sir, what can I say? It is simply excellent.”

footnotes.text: Taltala is situated next to Sealdah. At one time Taltala was famous for making sandals. Vidyasagar used to wear Taltala sandals. There is a story that once he was going to Burdwan by train. His fellow passenger was an Englishman. At one point, Vidyasagar felt drowsy. After some time, when he opened his eyes he noticed that his sandals had vanished. He realized that the Englishman had played a practical joke on him by throwing the sandals out through the window. After some time the Englishman went to the toilet, leaving his coat behind. Vidyasagar quietly put the coat out of the window and threw it away. On his return, the Englishman asked “Where is my coat?” Vidyasagar answered, “Your coat has gone in search of my sandals.”

paragraphs.text: Medicine kills disease. That is why one of the etymological meanings of the word tha that we get by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root thurva is “medicine”. In this sense, “medicine” does not refer only to diseases of the body but also to diseases to the mind. One medicine for mental disease is to lighten the mind by inducing pleasant feelings, the purpose being to remove tension and anxiety. This is the reason why in ancient times there used to be a kind of person who kept people happy by using different kinds of humour so that their minds overflowed with joy. These people might not have been very educated or scholarly but they were definitely experts in human psychology. These people were called jesters. Your must be quite familiar with the abstract noun, vaeduśya [jest].

paragraphs.text: There was once an Englishman with a bright red complexion and an unforgettable name. His full name was possibly Mr. Butterbread Laughingstock. That Englishman once travelled the whole world in search of a famous talker. He went around the world for the second time in search of a famous jester. On his first trip, the people of Bengal encouraged him. Thinking that the Bengalis would encourage him the second time as well, he went to Kolkata. The first time, when he went to China and met the most famous talker of that place, he came to know, on enquiry, that his name was Mr. Gu Ling. From there he flew to London ( 1 )Heathrow airport on a non-stop flight. After speaking to many eminent talkers of England, he came in contact with Sardar Bacan Bagiish [the greatest talker]. On asking his name, he came to know that his name was Mr. Gulist [the word gul, a slang in Bengali, means “a lie”]. From there he went to Paris ( 2 ), the capital of France. There, after making acquaintance with the famous talkers of the place he came in contact with the highest award-winning talker, whose name was Monsieur Gulon. From there he went to Berlin ( 3 ). On being introduced to the greatest talker of the place, who was also a noted film star he came to know that his name was Herr Guler. From there he went to Roma ( 4 ), the capital of Italy ( 5 ). On reaching there he enquired about their greatest talker and it did not take much time to find him. On enquiry he learned that his name was Signor Gulini. Next he went to Moscova ( 6 ).

During the period of apprenticeship you will be temporarily named Udaygulu Vidyarthii [a neophyte of fibbing]”.

paragraphs.text: Cakito Cakkotti returned to Camripota after his trip to Britain. He used to work at a railway office in Sealdah and commute from Camripota daily. Every day he was late in reaching his office. He used to reach by the last local train. One day he decided, “Tomorrow I shall make an historic exception, I must go to Sealdah by the first local train. If I canʼt go I shall change my name to Sacakita ( 12 ) Cakkotti.” The next morning, on waking up, Cakito Cakkotti looked at his wrist watch and saw that it was 7.35. He would have to finish everything quickly, and he thought, “Itʼs only twenty-five to eight, so there is enough time in hand. Let me have my morning tea in bed. Today I must do everything by the clock.” He again looked at his watch, “Twenty-five to eight. Thereʼs enough time. Let me read the newspaper. Today I wonʼt budge an inch from the hands of the clock. Let me see what the time is. Oh, itʼs just seven thirty-five. Thereʼs enough time. On this winter day, let me thoroughly massage some mustard oil on my body and bask in the sun. Today, I should be called Gharimáná Cakkotti [Cakkotti, the absolutely punctual one] instead of Cakito Cakkotti. Oh, I am surprised to see how steadily I am keeping a watch on the clock. Let me see, what time is it?

Adjacent to it is the village of Changripota, from which the great scholar, Manabendranath Roy (Narendranath Bhattacharya) originated. Kodalia, the ancestral home of Subhas Chandra Bose is very close by. Kodalia has now been renamed Subhasgram.

Literally, “A jewel recognises another jewel”, just as a hog instinctively finds taro (kacu).

The word biláyet means an overseas country. In the course of time, people took bilet to mean Britain, though in fact, all overseas countries may be described as bilet. The Persian word for Britain is not biláyet but bartaniá. In Urdu it would be hukumat-e-bartaniá. The Sanskrit word lanká also means the same thing – a piece of land surrounded by water. Sri Lanka or Ceylon is also surrounded by water, so it was called Lanka in Sanskrit.

paragraphs.text: We get two words, daḿshana and dashana by adding the suffix anat́ to the verbal root daḿsha. The word daḿshana means “to bite”. Dashana means “tooth” because people bite with their teeth. You can use the words danta, data or dashana, because each of them means dáṋt [tooth]. A person whose teeth are as white as jasmine may be described as kundadanta, kundadashana or kundadata. For the feminine gender one can use kundadantii or kundadashaná. However, the word kundadatii is most in use.

paragraphs.text: In my childhood we used to hear a ghost story of two female ghosts who were always vigorously quarrelling with each other. They used to fight all the time. They were actually nanad-bháj [nanad: husbandʼs sister; bhaj: brotherʼs wife],that is, sisters-in-law. One was called Mrs. Kulokarnii ( 1 ), because her ears were as big as a kulo [a bamboo winnowing tray], and the other was called Mrs. Muladantii (grammatically, muladatii would have been more appropriate), because her teeth were as big as radishes. One was holding a handbag made of scorpion skin, while the other had a handbag made of the bones of large black ants. When these two ladies used to quarrel, while grasping their handbags and looking at the sky all the while, it was such a wonderful sight that it simply defies any description.

paragraphs.text: A photographer from Phurphura once told me that he had tried religiously as many as one thousand, one hundred and eleven times, counting each attempt on his fingers, to capture the scene with his technicolour video camera. But every time, he had returned disappointedly from Baratajpur, because both the female ghosts had chased him away with a stubby broom. Mrs. Kulokarniiʼs husband, Mr. Pindigela Bhut (P.G.B. for short) used to roam about in the fields and forests, among shrubs, bushes, bamboo groves and shyáoŕá trees, in order to escape the cacophony of those quarrels. paragraphs.text: When somebody wears an affected smile conspicuously revealing their teeth, while suppressing their actual feelings, it is called dáshanikatá ( 1 ) in Sanskrit. While etymologically the word da , formed by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root dam is dáshanikatá, meaning “the smile of a person baring their teeth, while suppressing their actual feelings”, the word, in a general sense, indicates a situation where one supports somebody in public without actually supporting them in oneʼs heart. If somebody, while actually happy, sheds crocodile tears, that is also called dáshanikatá. This dáshanikatá is only another name for deceptive behaviour. Many of you have personal experience of dáshanikatá. I also have such experience. Let me tell you about one or two such small incidents in this connection.
summary: When somebody wears an affected smile conspicuously revealing their teeth, while suppressing their actual feelings, it is called dáshanikatá ( 1 ) in Sanskrit

paragraphs.text: In North India most people are Vaeśńavas [worshippers of Viśńu], while a few are Shaevas [worshippers of Lord Shiva]. There are hardly any worshippers of Shakti [the goddess Káli], the Sun or Gańapati [lord Ganesh]. Among the Vaeśńavas, the devotees of Sita-Ram outnumber the devotees of Radhe-Shyam [Radha and Krśńa]. Since there are more votaries of Sita-Ram than of Radhe-Shyam, one gets more opportunity to hear the word Sita-Ram than Radhe-Shyam in the streets. Those who want to hear Radhe-Shyam therefore have recourse to a ruse. If, on seeing them, the small boys of the locality say “Sita-Ram, Sita-Ram”, they say, “Sánanda raho bet́á, sánanda raho” [Be happy, my child, be happy]. And if the small boys, on seeing them, say “Radhe-Shyam, Radhe-Shyam” they pretend to be angry and chase them away. The small boys retrace a few steps in fear and then again start taunting, “Radhe-Shyam”. In this clever way, the person gets the opportunity to hear their favourite name, “Radhe-Shyam”.

paragraphs.text: Dandabhukti has not received as much recognition in history as Bardhaman bhukti has, for various reasons. For some unknown reason, historians did not pay any great attention to Dandabhukti. If somebody wants to write the history of Dandabhukti they will see that there is so much material that if properly organized, one can write several Mahábháratas. As many famous people were born in this region, similarly there are also innumerable towns and villages of great cultural heritage here. Towards the end of the Pathan period Dandabhukti was renamed Hijli, and towards the end of the Moghul period its name was changed to Madinápur. When the British got the civil rights of Bardhaman, 24 Parganas and Chattagram, along with Madinápur, they renamed it Midnapore. In the course of time its Bengali name became Medinipur. The district, which is very large, has also made such a significant contribution to the art of town planning and civilization, not only to the entire Ráŕh region but also to the entire civilized world that it is a veritable seat of human civilization. The sea that skirts it and the range of hills that border the district, sloping from north-west to the south-east, led to a magnificent opulence of all kinds of earthly treasures. Starting with Kalidas, the great poet, many great people were born in this district. In the Buddhist period, Dantapurivihár of this district, the present name of which is Dáṋton, was built upon the place where a receptacle containing the relics of the Buddhaʼs teeth – lay buried. It is here that Sarashaḿka, the most beautiful water tank, not only of the Ráŕh region but also of the entire Bengal, is situated.

In undivided Bengal, Nadia had five subdivisional towns: Krishnanagar, the district headquarters, Ranaghat, Meherpur, Chuadanga and Kusthia. At the time of partition, Nadia District was divided into two: Krishnanagar Sadar and Ranaghat subdivisional towns were included in India, and the subdivisional town of Kusthia became part of Pakistan. Of the four police station areas of Meherpur subdivisional town, Karimpur and Tehatta became Indian territory, and Meherpur and Gangni became part of Pakistan. Of the five police station areas of Chuadanga, Krishnganj became part of India and the other four police stations, that is, Chuadnga, Alamdanga, Damurhuda and Jibannagar, became part of Pakistan. In the beginning, the part of Nadia District included in Pakistan retained the name Nadia and the district headquarters were in Kusthia. The part of Nadia retained in India was named Nabadwip District, and the district headquarters continued to be in Krishnanagar. After some time, the name of Pak-Nadia district was changed to Kusthia District. Then, the name of the Indian district of Nadia was again changed from Nabadwip District back to Nadia District. From the Moghul period, the district headquarters of Nadia District was Goari-Krshnanagar. However, the capital of the Maharaja of Nadia was in Gangni in the beginning (during the time of Ram Samaddar and Kali Samaddar], later it was in Matiari and then in Rewi. The name of the village of Rewi was later changed to Krishnanagar. The two villages, Goari and Ghurni, adjacent to Krishnanagar, were already there. It was Allal Dastur Pir who did the town planning for Krishnagar.
The land formed by nine islands that surfaced from the ocean in very ancient times was named Navadvipa (nine islands), navadvipa > naodiiá > nadiiá > nade.

Most of our original plantains came into existence as a result of experimentation with different kinds of seedy plantains. Compared to our familiar plantains like cáṋpá, martmán, ciniicáṋpá, kánáibáshi, málbhog, dudhiyá, the káṋt́álii kalá [káṋt́álii plantain] is somewhat of recent origin. It originated from the seedy plantain some 2000 years ago, during the Buddhist period in Bengal. In size, it is slightly bigger than the cáṋpá plantain. Unlike cáṋpá kalá it has costae [ridges] on the skin. The cáṋpá kalá tastes a little sour, particularly after sunset, but that is not the case with káṋt́álii kalá. If properly cultivated, cáṋpá kalá yields twice a year, while káṋt́álii kalá yields twice in a year and a half. If uncared for, cáṋpá kalá remains cáṋpá kalá; only its size is reduced. But the káṋt́álii kalá, if not properly taken care of, becomes a seedy plantain again. This means that its relation with the seedy plantain has not yet been severed.

paragraphs.text: In our locality lived Mr Pulakita Ray (Pulakita: he used to pronounce it pulkit), a Hindi teacher. In my childhood, teachers were addressed as mát́ár sáháb [Honʼble Sir] in Bihar. Pulakita Ray knew no English, and I have no idea of his proficiency in Hindi. He used to go the class wearing a dirty dhuti [loin cloth] raised above his knees, a phatuá [a kind of loose cotton waistcoat] full of betel leaf stains, and a gámchá [cotton napkin] on his shoulders. He used to carry a matchbox in one pocket and a bundle of biŕi in another pocket of the phatuá. He used to split each matchstick into two, lengthwise, so that he could get double the matchsticks originally in the matchbox. Immediately on reaching the school, the mát́ár sáháb used to take a bath at the adjacent tube well and then used to take chátu ( 1 ) [flour generally made of roasted chickpeas] (Sanskrit for cholár chátu is shaktu, and chátu made of barley or muŕi [parched rice] is called dhánáká or dhánácurńa in Sanskrit).

paragraphs.text: Since I was a Brahminʼs daughter I could not be married twice. My grandmother slapped me on the cheek and said, “You miserable wretch [literally, ‘burnt-faced one’]! Why were you born into the house of a Brahmin? It is on account of this that you have to suffer so much. The elder brothers of my husband were ninety-two years old and above, and the younger brothers of my husband were then above sixty years old. They were talking amongst themselves, 'If we allow this one to survive she will enjoy the property; it doesnʼt matter whether she can buy or sell it. So it is better to burn this horrid girl along with her husband on the same funeral pyre, and make her a sati ( 2 ) [a widow who burns herself on her husbandʼs pyre]. Let this pitiable creature go to heaven and enjoy rice and fish ad infinitum. Scorched by the fire, I cried aloud and tried to jump off the pyre and run away. But the brothers of my husband fixed me to a bamboo cane and burnt me to death, having already tied up my hands and feet. They poured a lot of vermilion on the spot where they had burnt me and marked it as a secret place of sati and said, ”Ah! What a pious girl she was; she became a sati smilingly, at the age of three. Even now the girls of the village, before putting a vermilion mark on the forehead, touch the spot with a pinch of vermilion and pray, 'May I also become a sati like her.ʼ But do you know, t́hákurpo [husbandʼs younger brother]? These days, they [the widows] never become sati at the death of their husband. On the contrary, they take out the bunch of keys from their husbandʼs pocket and keep it in their own custody. Well, my t́hákurpo, in a weak, unguarded moment I talked my heart out to you. Since that time I have been living in this mango tree as a female ghost and I have decided to tell the tale of my sorrow to educated and cultured people whenever I come across them. And I shall request that the notorious scoundrels of society who have perpetrated inhuman barbarism in the name of the welfare of the society, and continue to do so, should be taken to task.”

In that dark age, only in three cases were women spared the sahamarańa [burning together, to burn oneself to death on the funeral pyre of oneʼs husband]: (1) if a woman was pregnant, (2) if the woman had a child to be breast fed (3) if the woman happened to be at her parentsʼ place at the time of the death of her husband and her parents, out of compassion, did not give her permission to die on the funeral pyre of her husband. According to the Mahábhárata Madri followed the death of her husband, Pandu by dying on his funeral pyre. Kunti took charge of the sons of Madri - Nakul and Sahadeb – in addition to her own sons, Yudhisthir, Bhima and Arjuna. The institution of sati was in practice only in those communities where there was no provision for widow-remarriage.

You had never seen Rs. 3000 at a time since your birth. On coming here you saw it and it went to your head. From today onwards, donʼt introduce yourself as a female ghost because that will only provoke peopleʼs laughter. Furthermore, it is not true that your husband really earns Rs. 3000 per month. His actual salary is just barely Rs. 1000, and the rest he manages by smuggling bed sheets, towels, medicines and phenyl from the hospital to the black market. paragraphs.text: The inherent weaknesses which harm humans are called ripus [enemies]. And the kind of constraints that attack a human by taking opportunity of these ripus and oppress him like a millstone around his neck, are called pásha. The ripus are six in number: káma [desire], krodha [anger], lobha [avarice], mada [pride or vanity], moha [blind attachment], mátsarya [jealousy]; and the bonds which bind a person on account of the presence of these ripus are called páshas [pásha means bandhanarajju ( 1 ) or bondage]. They are eight in number:

paragraphs.text: Thus, hatred, doubt, fear, shyness, censure, vanity of lineage, cultural superiority complex, and egotism are the eight bondages. The biijamantra [acoustic root] of the bondage of hatred is pa. A bond does not necessarily relate to only one ripu; it can involve several. However, the bondages of hatred and fear, in spite of their association with other ripus are mainly related to the ripu of attachment. Suppose somebody is addicted to drinking. The mind moves downward when the attraction is materialistic. The verb pat [patati] is used for the downward motion. The addiction leads to oneʼs fall. And when the motion is upward it is called anurakti and the ultimate form of anurakti is called bhakti [devotion]. This is the reason why the verb in Sanskrit for such movement is urdhva gam (urdhvagacchati). One who has the weakness of an addiction to drinking becomes easily bound by hatred and fear. Not only addiction to drinking, any kind of attachment makes one both detestable to others and afraid of others. One runs after a delusion without any rhyme or reason. This idea of attachment brings a story to my mind.

paragraphs.text: An acquaintance of mine lived in Mominpur – I canʼt exactly recollect his name, possibly it was Mańd́ámohon Mukhujje. Some people called Mandamohan an extremely niggardly miser, some said he was a myopic miser, some said he was so closefisted that even water would not pass through his fingers. Some said that if he had to spend even one pice, he would feel as if he had broken a rib; some said that he was “one pice father, mother” [for him, to part with even a single pice is like to give up his father or mother], some said he was “one pice pyáṋjphulurii [onion vegetable chop]”, some humourously called him pyáṋj-payjár. Modern boys called him “upurhasta no-not-never” [he who never extends his hand in a giving gesture, one who never gives anything]. He immensely enjoyed all these appellations.

paragraphs.text: That year there was an overproduction of brinjal. The farmers in a country where there is no scientific economic structure become practically ruined when there is an over production. That year, the farmers of Bengal were practically ruined on account of the over production of brinjal. Once, I went to the village of Bego under the Haringhata Police Station in Nadia District and there I saw that the farmers where cutting brinjal into pieces and, after adding some salt, giving them to the cows. As soon as a cow which was about to eat it noticed that it was brinjal, it turned its face away and said humbá humbá. As it tried to take its food from another part of the pot, it saw brinjal there also and again it refused to eat. The farmers realized that if the cows stopped eating fodder they would not yield any milk, so they stopped serving brinjal to the cows.

paragraphs.text: The farmers of Ramnagar of Birbhum District were traditional cultivators of brinjal. On going there I heard that they had stopped plucking the brinjal from the plants. They told me, “Sir, let the brinjal rot on the plants. It will be more useful as compost.” I could not go to Panjipara for lack of time, so I cannot say what happened to the famous brinjal of that place. In those days, articles were sold in the wholesale market in our town in pasurii. Five seers made one pasurii and eight pasuriis made one mund. But there was no uniform measure of seer in all the districts. A standard seer meant eighty tolás [1 tola is 11.664 grams, so a standard seer would be 933.12 grams]. But in our Monghyr District a seer was eighty four tolas. Again, in the neighbouring district of Bhagalpur, it varied from a hundred, a hundred and one, and a hundred and three tolás in different places. In some places, a seer was even a hundred and five tolás.

paragraphs.text: Once, in our locality, preparations for Kali Puja [worship of the goddess Káli] were being made with great pomp and show. Some boys were busy with theatre rehearsals. Some of them felt an acute shortage of money. Earlier, they used to manage some money from the shopping expenses of the family, but now, on account of growing expenses, their father started doing the shopping, himself. To combat the resultant lack of commission, some of the overenthusiastic boys started going around collecting subscriptions. People paid subscriptions according to their capacity. When Mańd́ámahon was asked to pay a subscription, he was visibly shocked. He said, “Oh God, you are talking about Kali! She is a great, belligerent lady, and we are devout Vaeśńavas. We canʼt worship Kali, it is forbidden by our ancestors.”

footnotes.text: Rajju is a loanword in Sanskrit. There is no appropriate etymological explanation for it. There is no need to rack oneʼs brain in search of its etymology.
To eat harimat́ar means not to eat anything.

In Bihar, those who sell vegetables are called kujrás, and those who cultivate vegetables are called koiriis. The koiriis are Hindus, while kujrás are Muslims. The mother tongue of the kujrás of our locality was Auṋgiká. There names used to be Maharaj Kujra, Shanicara Kujra, Etobari Kujra, and so on.

paragraphs.text: A story which is historically famous comes to my mind. The name of the village was Kuŕiye Kháoyá [eating leftovers]. Mr. Kipt́ekaiṋjus Kar [Kipt́e means “an extremely miserly person”] was a famous man of that place. Kipt́ekaiṋjus used to earn a lot of money in various legal and illegal ways. It dawned on him that if he wanted to suddenly become rich, it would be necessary to get a boon from Lord Shiva. To please other gods, it is necessary to perform a long and difficult penance. But Shiva is Bholanath [one who easily forgets peopleʼs misdeeds] and Ashutośa [One who is easily satisfied]. He becomes happy even if one offers him one ákanda flower [Calotropis gigantea] and a few leaves of the bel [Aegle marmelos] tree. So he decided to worship him.

paragraphs.text: Kipt́ekaiṋjus travelled on. He was not afraid of tigers, nor of snakes, nor of crocodiles emerging from the water. He was lost in thoughts of wealth; this strong attachment blurred his vision. He had no time to ponder what others would say or think. He walked on and on, through his extreme greed for money. Suddenly, something came into view and Kipt́ekaiṋjus stopped. He was not able to believe his eyes. In front of him there was a hill of cowries [kaŕi ( 2 )], on his right there was a mountain of cowries, on the left there was a hillock of cowries and at the back a mound of cowries. He declared victory. But whose victory? Not the victory of Shiva, nor the victory of Kuber. It was the victory of cowries.

paragraphs.text: In those days, there was no Rs.1 currency note. In the British period, the use of cowries was banned. Coins made of copper, bronze, or silver were mostly in use. (Gold coins with alloy, which are called sovereigns in English and gini in Bengali, from which we have the word ginisońá, were also used, though they were scarce.) That is why the shopkeepers, when going home from their shops, used to put their coins in a bundle and tightly tie them up so that they did not make any noise. The bundle of even a small merchant usually contained a large number of coins.

paragraphs.text: Once upon a time, a few dead crows were lying scattered about the hermitage of a fakir [a Muslim ascetic]. People asked him, “Fakir Saheb, why did so many forest crows die in the storm?” The Fakir replied, “The crows used to disturb me a lot. Yesterday evening I strongly warned them. I said to them, ‘f you donʼt behave properly I will finish you all offʼ. Just see, before a single night had passed, they all were struck dead by the storm. Had they followed my instruction and learnt to cuckoo instead of cawing, they would not have suffered such a fate.”

footnotes.text: The word arańyánii, means a large forest. Brhat him means him [snow] which is spread out to a great distance and in this sense it is called himánii [mass of snow]. But yavanánii does not mean brhat yavan; yavanánii means the script or writing of yavana. Although the word arańyánii is correct the word banánii is not correct.

Although there were many synonyms of kaŕi [cowrie] in Sanskrit, the two words, kat́iká and kathiká are most current. In ancient times, the cowrie was the main means of exchange used in commercial transactions. Copper coins were also in use, but their supply was not sufficient to meet the demands of the market at that time. There is no need to have a mint for manufacturing cowries, so they were freely used as currency. For very expensive articles, taḿkaka (t́áká) or raopyakam (rúpeyá) [silver coins] were used. Ordinary people did not have much connection with taḿkaka or raopyakam. In fact, sometimes the common people managed through bartering, instead of using cowries. In our childhood, the word adal badal [bartering] was extensively used in the Ráŕh region. In my childhood I saw the bartering of a kunke [a small measure] of rice in exchange for vegetables, fish, edible herbs, spinach, poppy seeds, salt, oil, and so on. I also saw, in the Khayrasol of Birbhum, how a carpenter exchanged handmade wooden lampstands for rice in the market place. The barter system of modern times is also something like this.

Támra > támba > támbá > táṋbá. In ancient India, coins were usually made of copper. This practice continued until the Moghul period. In the British period the use of pure copper for making coins was banned because it was not economic [the intrinsic value was more than the face value].

In ancient India, silver coins were [also] in use. A very few currency notes were printed, however. But coins [of higher value] were made of pure silver. During the British period, coins made of pure silver were in use for some time at the beginning, although some alloy was mixed in the coins. One could have an idea of the quantity of alloy by clanking the coins in oneʼs hand. The usable silver was called cáṋdi.

In ancient India, Persia and most countries of Asia, coins were made of pure gold; they were called kaiṋcana in Sanskrit. Kaiṋcana means “that gold which does not contain even an iota of alloy, gold which is not contaminated”. Alloyed gold or gini sońá originated in Europe and came to India during the British period.

The original word is bilva. One must use bargiiya ba [ba belonging to the class of twenty-five consonantal stops of Bengali alphabet]. Some of the synonyms are: iksváku, maháphalam, shriiphalam; the word bil means hole.

paragraphs.text: An enlightened human, resplendent with the brilliance of wisdom, was never so since the moment of his or her birth. Enlightenment and rationality free from dogmatic ideas come step by step at a certain stage of the rhythmic movement of the development of human consciousness through various impediments and constraints. I cannot say that the humans of today have become completely free from dogmas. In fact, the humans of today are yet to become free from superstitions. This is the reason why there are so many clashes, murders, quarrels, squabbles and misunderstandings among humans. Those who give the excuse of misunderstanding usually deliberately misunderstand or pretend to misunderstand in order to fulfill their own interests. Yet, the wisdom of the humans of earlier times must certainly have been less profound than that of the humans of today. Their lives were based on blind attachment to dogmas. Those superstitions of theirs, continuing for such a long time, have done a great injury to a large part of society, making it suffer the cataclysmic crisis of decadence. Those people who tried to control this decadence either died out, or somehow survived and trudged on with broken knees. The idea of the yakśa was one such superstition born out of dogmatic beliefs.

paragraphs.text: A yakśa [was considered to be] an assistant of Kuber [the god of wealth], so it would never allow wealth to go to waste. On the strength of this belief, people would build a small room under the earth, in which to keep their wealth. They would seat a young, dark-skinned boy there, in front of a lighted lamp, and perform some occult rites (this type of negative occult ritual is called pha). Then, on coming back above ground, they would cover the roof of that room with earth, camouflaging it with the adjoining land so that nobody would suspect anything from outside. After sometime, the flame of the lamp would go out, and simultaneously, the lamp of that innocent boyʼs life would also be extinguished. He would fall into an eternal slumber in the abyss of darkness.

They thought that he would be freed only after he had handed over the entire wealth to the rightful owner at the appropriate time. In Bengali, this type of wealth was called yakher dhan in common speech. In Bihar, the places which were known to have such wealth were called brhamasthán [the seat of Brahma]. Nobody likes to go to such places – in fact, people are afraid to go to such places after sunset.

paragraphs.text: Not only those innocent boys but also young, innocent dark-skinned girls were subjected to the atrocities of the superstitious process of making a yakśa. A wealthy man would dig a huge tank and keep his wealth at the bottom of it. A young, dark-skinned girl would have her hands and legs tied, and would be drowned in that tank, while occult rituals were performed (needless to say, this was also called pha). The moment the dead body of the girl surfaced, it was presumed that the dead girl had turned into a yakśińii [a female yakśa]. It was believed that when the rightful owner of that wealth would come to that tank in future, the yakśińii would hand over the wealth to him, and she would then become free. Such a yakśińii used to be called yakhe buŕii in the Bengali vernacular of that time. A tank where such macabre rituals were performed was called yakher pukur [a yakśaʼs tank] or tálpukur [a tank with palm trees]. Some people think that if the water in a tank is deep (tál is a measure of water, such as báṋo), then that tank is called a tálpukur. This is not wholly true. Palm trees were planted around a tank just to mislead people. There is a prevalent notion that in the event of a sudden need of a large number of utensils on account of some feast or yajiṋa [an elaborate worship], if a girl goes to that tank, stands in the neck-deep water and prays to the yakhe buŕii, then the following morning, the yakhe buŕii will supply the utensils and leave them on the bank of the tank. After the ceremonial function is over it is necessary to return the utensils after washing them clean, and leaving them on the bank of the tank. It is believed that if some greedy person steals those utensils, the yakhe buŕii will catch hold of their legs and drag them down to hell when they come to the tank again in future.

paragraphs.text: Báburám Bhar was his only son. You know the functions of five generations in regard to wealth. The first generation only buys property and collects wealth. So it may be called Kenárám [the buying generation]. The second generation enjoys the property, spends it in luxury and swaggers about in aristocratic style. It may be called Báburám [the luxurious generation]. The third generation maintains the same luxurious habits by selling the property. It may be called Becárám [the selling generation]. During the selling generation, the property practically becomes completely exhausted, and as a result the next generation spends its days in great hardship. So it may be called Dukhiirám [the suffering generation]. After Duhkhiirám, there is practically no property left, so the fifth generation takes to begging for a living. This may be called Bhikhurám [the begging generation]. So our Bhuṋŕobhombal was Kenárám and his only son was Báburám.

paragraphs.text: For his lunch and dinner, Bhuṋŕobhombal used to have newly harvested aush rice [rice made from paddy which ripens in the rainy season or autumn] with rice water. The new aush rice takes time to digest, so a little quantity fills the stomach. People used to ask him, “Why donʼt you strain the water from the rice?” He used to reply, “Doctors say that the water contains vitamins.” He used to eat burnt brinjals with boiled rice, because compared to fried brinjal, burnt brinjal needs very little oil, so little, in fact, that it can be burnt even without using any oil. He used to collect jujubes that had fallen from the tree, prepare a sour curry with them and eat it. When jujubes were not available he used to buy a few hog plums or tamarind and prepare a sour sauce, and felt very unhappy that he had to incur an additional expenditure. He felt uneasy during the day and could not sleep at night. After the expulsion of his son his expenditure was considerably reduced.

paragraphs.text: One day, he thought, “Who knows into whose extravagant hands my huge property will fall after my death?” He decided to bury his wealth under the ground and hand it over to a yakh [yakśa]. He thought that the yakh would hand over that wealth to the rightful heir or he would take it back from the yakh when he was reborn as a human being in his next birth. He did not look for a mason to construct the underground room in which to keep the wealth meant for the yakh. There were two reasons for this. The first and foremost reason was that the mason in that case would come to know about the hidden wealth. And the second reason was that it had often happened that cruel people had murdered the mason after their underground room had been constructed, so that the secret would not leak out. Once these crimes became public knowledge, masons were not willing to build underground rooms for hiding wealth. So Bhuṋŕobhombal started building the room himself with various necessary implements and building materials. It is not an easy job to make a room underground.

paragraphs.text: After some time, the room was finished. Bhuṋŕobhombal also took lessons from a negative occultist in the rituals to be performed for making a yakśa. However, it was difficult to find a young, dark-skinned boy. He avidly waited, like the crow of a sacred place, for a such a boy to come in the direction of his house, by chance. Even the beggar boys never came near his house because he never gave any alms. On the contrary, instead of getting alms they got a beating. One day, he saw that a dark-skinned boy of about five years old was passing by his house. He was wearing silver bangles. In Bengal, in those days, both men and women used to wear bangles. Both the children of well-to-do families as well as those of ordinary families used to wear golden bangles, while the poor ones used to wear bangles made of silver or bell metal. On seeing the boyʼs silver bangles, Bhuṋŕobhombal understood that the boy belonged to a poor family. He then tempted the boy with a treat of sweets and brought him within the compound of his house. Then he led him to the underground room, and lighting a lamp before him, started performing the occult rituals. We have already said that such a ritual is pha. The lamp was burning, flickering, and intermittently blazing up rather tremulously. The boy became afraid and wanted to go away. He started imploring and crying to be let go. But the impervious heart of Bhuṋŕobhombal did not melt. He left the boy there, and covered the room by spreading earth over it. Certainly, the lamp became extinguished after sometime, and the lamp of that boyʼs life was also extinguished forever. Bhuṋŕobhombal, full of joy, went back to his house. He was happy that at last a solution had been found for preserving his huge property. Today, fully satisfied, he would eat stale rice with a curry made of potato skins, then have a deep sleep.

points.title: “The actual significance of the word sáhitya [loosely, ‘literature’] is inherent in the w
points.prompt: Recall and explain from memory: “The actual significance of the word sáhitya [loosely, ‘literature’] is inherent in the word itself. Sáhitya is define
summary: “The actual significance of the word sáhitya [loosely, ‘literature’] is inherent in the word itself. Sáhitya is defined as that whose characteristic is to mov
points.body: “The actual significance of the word sáhitya [loosely, ‘literature’] is inherent in the word itself. Sáhitya is defined as that whose characteristic is to move with (sahita = “with”) the trends of life… The word sáhitya can be interpreted in another way as well: sa + hita = hitena saha, “that which co-exists with hita [welfare]”. Where there is no inner spirit of welfare, we cannot use the term sáhitya. The creations or compositions of those who proclaim, “Art for artʼs sake,” cannot be treated as sáhitya… Thus literature is that which moves together with society and leads society towards true fulfilment and welfare by providing the inspiration to serve. The statement “Art for artʼs sake” is not acceptable; rather we should say, “Art for service and blessedness.”… Those who are inferior and neglected, helpless and destitute – whom society considers to be infernal maggots – are the very people who are the most unrepresented in the salons of literature… The sáhityika or the artist has to take the responsibility of enabling them to rise up and sit in the same row with the rest of society, after dusting off the dirt from their bodies…

summary: The range and scope of short stories are exactly the same as those of plays, but short-story writers must know the technique of presenting a long story concisel
points.body: The range and scope of short stories are exactly the same as those of plays, but short-story writers must know the technique of presenting a long story concisely. Suspense is equally effective in short stories as in plays; dramatic skill is essential for the writer of those short stories which come in the category of sketches, because a sketch holds an intermediate position between a story and a play.”

points.body: In the unique and superb interpretation of sáhitya, literature, in terms of “Art for service and blessedness” given above, the author has provided eternal guidance to all those related to the world of literature. With the basic objectives set by the author, literature with all its branches, including plays and short stories, can truly build up an ideal and just society, which is the demand of the day.

points.title: Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar (also known as Shrii Shrii Ánandamúrti, a spiritual Guru) el
points.prompt: Recall and explain from memory: Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar (also known as Shrii Shrii Ánandamúrti, a spiritual Guru) elaborately explained his views
summary: Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar (also known as Shrii Shrii Ánandamúrti, a spiritual Guru) elaborately explained his views on art and literature in the discourse (
points.body: Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar (also known as Shrii Shrii Ánandamúrti, a spiritual Guru) elaborately explained his views on art and literature in the discourse (“The Practice of Art and Literature”, A Few Problems Solved Part 1) quoted from above. But he did not stop there. Advancing further, he translated his words into actions, creating a direct example in the form of his own literature, marked by his natural ease and aptitude. Thus we get a great series named Sarkarʼs Short Stories in fourteen parts. In June 1985, the first Bengali fourteen-part set was published under the authorʼs direct guidance. In January 1990, the English Sarkarʼs Short Stories Part 1 was published. Since then, there has been a persistent demand from our esteemed readers for the publication of all the parts. In response to that we are extremely happy to present to the readers now Sarkarʼs Short Stories Parts 1-3 in one volume. Genuine and sincere efforts are going on to publish all remaining parts within the next year. We fervently hope to fulfil this objective with the cooperation of all concerned.

points.title: All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as importan
points.prompt: Recall and explain from memory: All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as important and integral parts of the au
summary: All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as important and integral parts of the authorʼs writings on a vast domain of ling
points.body: All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as important and integral parts of the authorʼs writings on a vast domain of linguistics and philology which touched also on history, geography, medicine, science, art, religion, spirituality, philosophy, etc. Such books included Varńa Vijiṋána, Varńa Vicitrá (eight parts) and Shabda Cayaniká (twenty-six parts). Like most great authors, Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar is a consummate storyteller, thus he used in those books a seemingly inexhaustible supply of anecdotes, personal experiences and interesting as well as educative references, in order to capture the readerʼs interest. And it is mostly those stories that have been excerpted to constitute the present book. Thus it is natural that in the stories contained in the present book, we will find, either at the beginnings of those stories or as footnotes, relevant references to the linguistic and other subjects of the original books. In this way the stories retain the authenticity of the original books. Apart from the books mentioned above, some stories are from a volume of the authorʼs childrenʼs literature series – namely, In the Land of Hat́t́amálá.

points.body: Many readers are concerned that the authorʼs discourses, as published, should adhere as closely as possible to the precise wording the author used in speaking. For this reason, in the case of discourses given originally in English, the editors do not alter pronouns and other terms which the author in his lifetime considered “common-gender” words. As the author once said, “You know, ‘man’ is not only masculine gender, ‘man’ is common gender also. ‘Man is mortal’ – here ‘man’ means both male and female.”

In keeping with his guideline and with current trends, it is our policy in the case of translated discourses (where the published wording will necessarily be that of the translators) to use gender-neutral language.

points.body: Square brackets [ ] in the text are used to indicate translations by the editors or other editorial insertions. Round brackets ( ) indicate a word or words originally given by the author. When round brackets follow an English word or phrase and contain the equivalent Bengali word or phrase, it should be understood that the English words represent the English translation, while the contents of the brackets are the original Bengali words provided as extra information for the reader.

points.body: The author used a particular shorthand for explaining the etymologies of words. Under this system, a minus sign (–) follows a prefix, and a plus sign (+) precedes a suffix. Thus ava – tr + ghaiṋ = avatára can be read, “the root tr prefixed by ava and suffixed by ghaiṋ becomes avatára.”

Their sincere efforts are helping us to develop an ever more professional working system, so that the immense contribution of Shrii P.R. Sarkar can be presented in the best possible manner. Some esteemed lovers of Shrii Shrii Ánandamúrtiʼs (Shrii P.R. Sarkarʼs) books have come forward to make arrangements for the continuing publication of his books over the coming years; thanks to them, progress is being made in building up a committed and dependable sales network. In this regard, we welcome the participation and support of all.

summary: Every new translation is reviewed by a “first editor” who compares the English translation with the original Bengali or Hindi. Thereafter it is sent to the “sec
points.body: Every new translation is reviewed by a “first editor” who compares the English translation with the original Bengali or Hindi. Thereafter it is sent to the “second editors” to improve the standard of English. On completion of second editing, the final verification, which includes one more comparison with the original Bengali, is done by the Publication staff. Other important functions include the coordination of these different steps and the development and management of a global distribution and sales network.

summary: Human beings look for comfort. Thus the etymological meaning of the word d́ha that we get by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root d́huńd́a, is “instrument
points.body: Human beings look for comfort. Thus the etymological meaning of the word d́ha that we get by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root d́huńd́a, is “instrument of pleasure”; colloquially, it is called gadi [mattress or cushion]. Therefore gadi means “something which makes our lying or sitting comfortable”. The word d́ha can be used for the kind of cushion that we use under the mattress of a cot or the cushion that we use on a chair.

points.body: In North India, the word gaddá is generally used. But that does not mean that the word gaddii is not in use. However, in North and West India gaddii means “the place where the shopkeeper sits and looks after the office work or the accounts”; that is, the office. The office of various business enterprises is also called gaddii. The use of the word gaddii reminds me of the story of a merchant.

points.body: Sethjii [the merchant] was critically ill; he was on his death bed and the house was full of loud lamentation. On hearing the news of his imminent death the creditors became anxious. The debtors of Sethjii, on the other hand, had a slight glow on their faces, like the film of a thin cream of diluted milk. The children of Sethjii were terribly busy managing the matters related to the accounts of sales-tax, income-tax, excise-duty, and so on.

points.body: When Sethjii was about to breathe his last, all his seven children closed the gaddii [office] and stood by his death bed with folded hands. Sethjii started enquiring about their welfare by naming each of them. First he enquired about his eldest son. Sethjii asked, “Is Ramnajar present?” Ramnajar answered with folded hands, “Yes father, I am present”. Then he looked for the second son and asked, “Is Rampariikśań present?” Rampariikśań replied, “Yes, father, I am present.” Next he asked about the third son, “Is Ramsurath present?” Ramsurath responded, “Yes father, I am standing at your lotus feet”. Then Sethjii wanted to know about the fourth son, and asked, “Is Ramsiḿhásan present?” Ramsiḿhásan replied, “Yes father, your servant is present”. Then he enquired about the fifth son, “Is, Ramikbal present?” Ramikbal replied, “Yes father, I am standing at your feet.” Then he asked about the sixth son, “Is Rambeshan present?” Rambeshan answered, “Yes father, your servant is present”. Next he looked for the seventh son and asked, “Is Rananut́há present?” Rananut́há replied, “Your servant is here at your service.” Then the Sethjii flew into a rage and thundered, “If all seven brothers are present here then who is on the gaddii [who is looking after the office]?” As Sethjii started fuming and shouting his heart stopped and he died.

points.body: One who knows neither Hindi nor English may, on hearing Hindi, take it to be English. Also, on hearing English they may think it to be Hindi. The same kind of confusion may take place in relation to gadi and gaddii in Bengali and Hindi, respectively. When somebody says, Málik gaddii me háiṋ [The owner is in the office], a Bengali may take it to mean that the owner has been lying on the mattress of his bed. On the other hand, when a Bengali says, “Málik gadite shuye áche.” [The owner is sleeping on a mattress], someone who does not know Bengali may think that the owner is possibly lying on a bed in his shop.

The language of his umbilical cord [his mother tongue] was Auṋgiká. The language of his kitchen was Auṋgiká, the language of his house [the language of conversation of the inmates of the house] was Auṋgiká. After going to Patna, by conversing with his teachers and classmates, he had developed a good proficiency in Hindi. He also used to take part in Hindi plays. Then, during the summer holidays he came home. At noon he told his mother [in refined Hindi], “Mátah, myáṋy kśudhárta huṋ. Mujhe anna dená” [Mother, I am hungry; please give me some food].

points.body: The word d́hekur is derived from the word d́hekkar which means “to burp”. Sometimes the extravagance of intelligence is also described as d́hekure buddhi [burping intelligence]. Humans with d́hekure buddhi are intelligent but they cannot always maintain their balance. Luckily, the number of people with burping intelligence is always very small in every age and in every country. Yet, sometimes even these people with such intelligence do wonderful jobs. However, it is difficult to say whether this is due to the quality of their intelligence or just a fluke.

points.body: An oath-taking ceremony of ministers was to take place in some country of the world. It was to be held in the durbar ( 1 ) of the Governor of that place. The entire responsibility of supervising the ceremony was on the shoulders of this man with burping intelligence. The prospective ministers kept sitting with their heads tilted to one side, impatiently waiting for the auspicious moment of the oath-taking. They looked like those pots of date palm raw sugar kept on biṋd́e ( 2 ).They had donned new clothes, some had a mark of sandalwood paste on their foreheads and some had put marks of curd on their foreheads. Those who swaggered about as atheists did not put any mark on their forehead out of shyness, but hid a sanctified flower in their chest pockets and silently kept on chanting the name of their respective cherished deities, which “nobody will know about, nobody will hear.”

points.body: “Now, what happened was, a minister who did not know any English mistook MLA for an indigenous word and took the word to be eme le. You know that what is called is me [in something] in Hindi and er madhye in Bengali is called eme in the language of Bihar, and the word le simply means ”take“. The minister thought, eme le means ‘take in it’. That means, whatever you find, on any side – to your front or behind you, on the right or on the left, offered in gestures, in kind or cash, in this thing or that – just put it in your pocket. As the minister did not know the exact meaning of MLA he made his pocket so heavy that finally wicked people started accusing him of taking bribes. A mischievous commission also found him guilty of taking bribes. At last the minister lost his job. Anyway, please learn the exact meaning of MLA in advance. Donʼt pronounce it eme le.”

points.body: The d́hekure buddhimán further told the prospective ministers, “When you are going to the bathroom you can also use some perfume or put a cotton pad soaked in áttar [flower essence] into your ears because if the Governor expresses a desire to have a photograph taken with you, then the perfume on your body will emit a fine fragrance. Well, now let me teach you the regulations of protocol. Always assume a modesty of bearing, whether that modesty is needed or not. When you are served refreshments, donʼt start gobbling them up. However much temptation you may feel, you must resist it and eat slowly. If there is a salted snack on the plate, bite it in such a way that only a third of it goes into your mouth and two thirds are left behind. Again, if there are sweets on the plate, bite in such a way that only one fourth enters your mouth and three fourths are left behind on the plate. If you take tea or coffee, first pour it into a saucer and drink only half of it, leaving the rest on the saucer. Then, drink straight from the cup but you must stop as soon as you have finished half the cup, and leave the other half of the drink in the cup itself. After that, if you feel hungry you can take a bellyful of muŕi-begunpoŕá [parched rice and burnt brinjal] after returning home. If the Governor wonders, “Whatʼs the matter? You are not taking the refreshments. Is the food not palatable?” You will answer, “No, sir, the food is very good. It is actually our fault, because, always busy and engrossed in the thoughts of the welfare of the country as we are, we never get time to have refreshments. Not taking any refreshments for days on has become such a bad habit that we are now not able to consume even this delicious food.”

The word ta that we get by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root tan is used for “one who can express their ideas in music and dance”, and “acting and recitation”. So, in this case one of the meanings of the word ta is “an actor”. Sometimes an actor displays a strange presence of mind. In that sense he is a ta in both respects. There are many stories about the presence of mind or the nature of the presence of mind of these ta of the theatre world. I shall tell you one or two of such stories.

In brief, Sita was supposed to say, addressing the earth, “Oh mother earth, split open so that I can take a place in your lap.” Abdul Latif knew the drift of the play very well and he remembered most of the dialogues by heart. He also knew how he was to address mother earth at this point. But he had some confusion about the exact language of the dialogue. At that critical moment after he had just said, “Oh mother earth”, the prompter had a sudden bout of coughing. On account of the attack of coughing he was not able to speak, but “Sita” could not keep on standing with his mouth shut, waiting for him. He applied his presence of mind and said in the local dialect, “Mátah basundhare tui pháṋk ha, mui bhitarat dhukim”. [Mother earth, split – I want to go inside].

Various kinds of mannerisms of the actors and actresses (such as moving their hands and feet, some peculiar gestures and gesticulations, shaking the lips, turning the neck etc), defects of pronunciation (for example dyásh [for desh] kyábal [for kebal], onárá [for oṋŕá], cáikel [for sáikel], myágh [for megh], and malapropisms (mayávii in place of mayámay, nindak in place of ninduk) are easily detected during the rehearsals and can be rectified. It is therefore better not to believe those who say, “ekkere styáje áisyá dyaákhaiyá dimu ayáktiḿ káre kay” [Onstage, I shall show what acting really is]. It is better to have a thorough checking during the rehearsals.

points.body: Kusumkumari was a famous actress of that time. Her acting talents were simply superb but she would often be absent during rehearsals. This was the biggest problem with her. As a person Kusumkumari was very good and idealistic. The man of whom she was most fond had the surname “Biswas”, [meaning “faith”]. When this man surnamed Biswas died, Kusumkumari started eating only one meal a day as widows do. She would just have a simple vegetarian meal at noon. Everybody thought, “They must be highly talented and that is probably why we hear the applause and ‘Encore! Encore!’.” Sometime later these planted admirers used to call out, “Dádá ghurre phirre” [Brother, play it elaborately], to the tune of bala hari hari bol [“Utter the name of Hari again and again” – the chant accompanying a Hindu funeral procession]. points.body: In the Bengal of those days, every educated person was familiar with the book Niiladarpańa. Dinabandhu Mitra wrote this book based on the British exploitation of the indigo planters who cultivated indigo. Although well educated, Dinabandhu Mitra used to mix with the common people and was quite familiar with their feelings and language. He was a close friend of Bankimchandra. Once he came to a village in Jessorre [a district in the former undivided Bengal, now in Bangladesh] to get an idea of the peopleʼs opinion regarding his Niiladarpańa. He was crossing the river in a boat owned by someone called Hafij Mian. From the discussion of the crew he understood that the play Niiladarpańa had been staged in their village the previous night. They were discussing only this. He asked Hafiz Mian, “Well, brother, how was the play?” He replied, “Oh sir, what can I say? It is simply excellent.”

In this sense, “medicine” does not refer only to diseases of the body but also to diseases to the mind. One medicine for mental disease is to lighten the mind by inducing pleasant feelings, the purpose being to remove tension and anxiety. This is the reason why in ancient times there used to be a kind of person who kept people happy by using different kinds of humour so that their minds overflowed with joy. These people might not have been very educated or scholarly but they were definitely experts in human psychology. These people were called jesters. In the small hours of the morning the eldest brother went to the field with a gáŕu [ a pitcher or tankard with a spout, usually with a handle] in his hand, to get into a poetic mood. A gentle breeze was blowing, a poetic mood started coming to him, and the dark spots on the moon made it look like a slightly burnt chapati that had been overcooked. Then he suddenly noticed that there were three holes in front him, and there was water in all three holes, reflecting a moon in each, and there was one more in the sky. So, there were altogether four moons on earth. The eldest brother felt sudden poetic inspiration and wrote a line, Candra cáru [Four moons]. The eldest brother returned home hastily with the gáŕu [water pot] in hand and told his brothers, “Iʼve got it! Eureka, eureka! Now a fine one-line verse is on my lips.”

points.body: There was once an Englishman with a bright red complexion and an unforgettable name. His full name was possibly Mr. Butterbread Laughingstock. That Englishman once travelled the whole world in search of a famous talker. He went around the world for the second time in search of a famous jester. On his first trip, the people of Bengal encouraged him. Thinking that the Bengalis would encourage him the second time as well, he went to Kolkata. The first time, when he went to China and met the most famous talker of that place, he came to know, on enquiry, that his name was Mr. Gu Ling. From there he flew to London ( 1 )Heathrow airport on a non-stop flight. After speaking to many eminent talkers of England, he came in contact with Sardar Bacan Bagiish [the greatest talker]. On asking his name, he came to know that his name was Mr. Gulist [the word gul, a slang in Bengali, means “a lie”]. From there he went to Paris ( 2 ), the capital of France. There, after making acquaintance with the famous talkers of the place he came in contact with the highest award-winning talker, whose name was Monsieur Gulon. From there he went to Berlin ( 3 ). On being introduced to the greatest talker of the place, who was also a noted film star he came to know that his name was Herr Guler. From there he went to Roma ( 4 ), the capital of Italy ( 5 ). On reaching there he enquired about their greatest talker and it did not take much time to find him. On enquiry he learned that his name was Signor Gulini. Next he went to Moscova ( 6 ).

On arriving at Kolkata he saw that here were fibbing experts galore. In the streets and restaurants they were available in plenty. They were not prepared to recognize him as a fibbing expert. They told this Englishman, “Come and stay here as an apprentice in acquiring the art of fibbing. At that time, Cakitacakor was selling fish that he had caught in the pond, to an agent from the town. points.body: Cakitocakor said, “You have only dealt in selling fish but you have never done any research on them. Had you done so, you would have realized that there is not a single khayrá, kharsolá or cunopuṋt́i in this pond. I arranged a meeting with the well-known traditional fishermen on the bank of this pond. They all gave the unanimous verdict that the fish of this pond, which are thought to be puṋt́i fish, are actually the offspring of rui fish [a kind of very delicious freshwater fish, Labio rohita]. And the fish thought to be khayrá are actually the offspring of ilish [hilsa fish]. Here, the great sage Durbasa once expressed his desire to have a dish of rui fish with mustard seed paste and a hot broth of hilsa fish. The sage, sitting on a kush-mat and having performed the necessary ritual before lunch, anxiously waited [in Bengali this is called ha-pityesh ( 8 )] for the food. Impatiently, he started counting time but the hot fish broth never arrived. The villagers said, “We donʼt want to be drowned in an ocean of sin by feeding fish to the sage”.

Today, I should be called Gharimáná Cakkotti [Cakkotti, the absolutely punctual one] instead of Cakito Cakkotti. Oh, I am surprised to see how steadily I am keeping a watch on the clock. points.body: We get two words, daḿshana and dashana by adding the suffix anat́ to the verbal root daḿsha. The word daḿshana means “to bite”. Dashana means “tooth” because people bite with their teeth. You can use the words danta, data or dashana, because each of them means dáṋt [tooth]. A person whose teeth are as white as jasmine may be described as kundadanta, kundadashana or kundadata. For the feminine gender one can use kundadantii or kundadashaná. However, the word kundadatii is most in use.

points.body: In my childhood we used to hear a ghost story of two female ghosts who were always vigorously quarrelling with each other. They used to fight all the time. They were actually nanad-bháj [nanad: husbandʼs sister; bhaj: brotherʼs wife],that is, sisters-in-law. One was called Mrs. Kulokarnii ( 1 ), because her ears were as big as a kulo [a bamboo winnowing tray], and the other was called Mrs. Muladantii (grammatically, muladatii would have been more appropriate), because her teeth were as big as radishes. One was holding a handbag made of scorpion skin, while the other had a handbag made of the bones of large black ants. When these two ladies used to quarrel, while grasping their handbags and looking at the sky all the while, it was such a wonderful sight that it simply defies any description.

points.body: A photographer from Phurphura once told me that he had tried religiously as many as one thousand, one hundred and eleven times, counting each attempt on his fingers, to capture the scene with his technicolour video camera. But every time, he had returned disappointedly from Baratajpur, because both the female ghosts had chased him away with a stubby broom. Mrs. Kulokarniiʼs husband, Mr. Pindigela Bhut (P.G.B. for short) used to roam about in the fields and forests, among shrubs, bushes, bamboo groves and shyáoŕá trees, in order to escape the cacophony of those quarrels. When the other ghosts asked him, “Hayaṋ gáṋ tumi saṋv saṋmay baṋŕiir báṋire báṋire kenaṋ tháṋka gáṋ?” ( 2 ) [Hello, why do you always stay away from your house?] He would reply, “Áṋmáṋr haṋrt́er baṋyámoṋ áṋche kinṋaṋ, táṋi dáṋktár baṋleṋecheṋ khoṋlá háṋoyáy tháṋkteṋ.” [Since I have cardiac trouble, the doctor has advised me to remain in the open air].

points.body: When somebody wears an affected smile conspicuously revealing their teeth, while suppressing their actual feelings, it is called dáshanikatá ( 1 ) in Sanskrit. While etymologically the word da , formed by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root dam is dáshanikatá, meaning “the smile of a person baring their teeth, while suppressing their actual feelings”, the word, in a general sense, indicates a situation where one supports somebody in public without actually supporting them in oneʼs heart. If somebody, while actually happy, sheds crocodile tears, that is also called dáshanikatá. This dáshanikatá is only another name for deceptive behaviour. Many of you have personal experience of dáshanikatá. I also have such experience. Let me tell you about one or two such small incidents in this connection.
