points.body: In North India most people are Vaeśńavas [worshippers of Viśńu], while a few are Shaevas [worshippers of Lord Shiva]. There are hardly any worshippers of Shakti [the goddess Káli], the Sun or Gańapati [lord Ganesh]. Among the Vaeśńavas, the devotees of Sita-Ram outnumber the devotees of Radhe-Shyam [Radha and Krśńa]. Since there are more votaries of Sita-Ram than of Radhe-Shyam, one gets more opportunity to hear the word Sita-Ram than Radhe-Shyam in the streets. Those who want to hear Radhe-Shyam therefore have recourse to a ruse. If, on seeing them, the small boys of the locality say “Sita-Ram, Sita-Ram”, they say, “Sánanda raho bet́á, sánanda raho” [Be happy, my child, be happy]. And if the small boys, on seeing them, say “Radhe-Shyam, Radhe-Shyam” they pretend to be angry and chase them away. The small boys retrace a few steps in fear and then again start taunting, “Radhe-Shyam”. In this clever way, the person gets the opportunity to hear their favourite name, “Radhe-Shyam”.

points.body: In our locality lived Mr Pulakita Ray (Pulakita: he used to pronounce it pulkit), a Hindi teacher. In my childhood, teachers were addressed as mát́ár sáháb [Honʼble Sir] in Bihar. Pulakita Ray knew no English, and I have no idea of his proficiency in Hindi. He used to go the class wearing a dirty dhuti [loin cloth] raised above his knees, a phatuá [a kind of loose cotton waistcoat] full of betel leaf stains, and a gámchá [cotton napkin] on his shoulders. He used to carry a matchbox in one pocket and a bundle of biŕi in another pocket of the phatuá. He used to split each matchstick into two, lengthwise, so that he could get double the matchsticks originally in the matchbox. Immediately on reaching the school, the mát́ár sáháb used to take a bath at the adjacent tube well and then used to take chátu ( 1 ) [flour generally made of roasted chickpeas] (Sanskrit for cholár chátu is shaktu, and chátu made of barley or muŕi [parched rice] is called dhánáká or dhánácurńa in Sanskrit).

Eating chátu with milk and mango is also both tasty and invigorating.) At night he used to take rice at home. One day I saw that Mr Pulakita Ray was going to school with a full size dhuti and punjábii [a loose fitting upper garment with no collar] (In North India a punjábii is called Báḿlá kurtá [a Bengali shirt], with no betel leaf in his mouth and no matchbox in his pocket. I asked, “Kii holo che mát́ár sahib?” [“Whatʼs the matter today, sir?”]

Since candrabindu is not much in use amongst the common people, it is used in the nasalized articulation of a ghost to differentiate between a human and a ghost. This is just the opposite of French. The French language is dominated by nasalization.

points.body: The other day I was talking to Bankachand Baṋŕujje [Banerjee ( 1 )] of Bansbere. He had once gone to Champdani to buy a fishing hook made of bell metal. On the way there he came to wide open space without any locality nearby. It was completely desolate. Evening was fast approaching and it gave him an eerie feeling. Then he came to Goruti (Gaurhát́i) forest. After he had gone a few steps he saw a huge mango tree, and noticed that Gauṋgá [the Ganges] was nearby. There were crocodiles in the river and tigers in the forest, so he climbed up to the topmost branches of the tree, still trembling in fear. The evening was quickly turning to night. Suddenly, he noticed that just a little below him, sitting on a thick branch, a woman was kneading some dough. The woman asked him, “Tumi keṋ gáṋ, eṋi ráṋt biṋrete maṋgd́áṋle uṋt́he baṋsecha háoyá khete, áṋámáder eṋkheṋe páṋrk-táṋrk neṋi baṋt́e kintu beṋrábár maṋta baṋŕa báṋŕa bháṋgáŕ toń áṋche, seṋkháne háṋoyá kheṋte geṋle, náṋ kena gáṋ? [Who are you that you have come for fresh air by climbing up to the topmost branches of the tree, at night? It is true that there is no park or places like that here, but there are many big wastelands for a stroll. Why didnʼt you go there for some fresh air?”

points.body: Baudi said, “My in-lawʼs are from the west, in Balarambati. My father is from Baidyabati, my maternal uncle is from Sibarambati, my fatherʼs sister is from Janai and my motherʼs sister is from Bhandarhati. I was married at the age of three. At the time of the marriage I was sucking the breast of my maternal grandmother. My husband was 87. He was an aristocratic Brahmin – kávya, vyákarańa, sáḿkhya, vedánta tiirtha, tarkacaiṋcu, tarkapaiṋmcánan [a great scholar of poetry, drama, the Vedas, philosophy, Vedanta and logic]. After our marriage, when the married women were blowing conch shells, my husband felt trepidation in his chest on account of the sound of the conch shells and died of cardiac arrest. While I was still lying on the lap of my grandmother, I became a widow.

points.body: Since I was a Brahminʼs daughter I could not be married twice. My grandmother slapped me on the cheek and said, “You miserable wretch [literally, ‘burnt-faced one’]! Why were you born into the house of a Brahmin? It is on account of this that you have to suffer so much. The elder brothers of my husband were ninety-two years old and above, and the younger brothers of my husband were then above sixty years old. They were talking amongst themselves, 'If we allow this one to survive she will enjoy the property; it doesnʼt matter whether she can buy or sell it. So it is better to burn this horrid girl along with her husband on the same funeral pyre, and make her a sati ( 2 ) [a widow who burns herself on her husbandʼs pyre]. Let this pitiable creature go to heaven and enjoy rice and fish ad infinitum. Scorched by the fire, I cried aloud and tried to jump off the pyre and run away. But the brothers of my husband fixed me to a bamboo cane and burnt me to death, having already tied up my hands and feet. They poured a lot of vermilion on the spot where they had burnt me and marked it as a secret place of sati and said, ”Ah! What a pious girl she was; she became a sati smilingly, at the age of three. Even now the girls of the village, before putting a vermilion mark on the forehead, touch the spot with a pinch of vermilion and pray, 'May I also become a sati like her.ʼ But do you know, t́hákurpo [husbandʼs younger brother]? These days, they [the widows] never become sati at the death of their husband. On the contrary, they take out the bunch of keys from their husbandʼs pocket and keep it in their own custody. Well, my t́hákurpo, in a weak, unguarded moment I talked my heart out to you. Since that time I have been living in this mango tree as a female ghost and I have decided to tell the tale of my sorrow to educated and cultured people whenever I come across them. And I shall request that the notorious scoundrels of society who have perpetrated inhuman barbarism in the name of the welfare of the society, and continue to do so, should be taken to task.”

points.body: One day, I was wondering what could be the suitable Bengali for the phrase used above. While thinking about it, I was passing Belun, a village in Hooghly district. Evening had just fallen. Suddenly, I noticed that two tall women were shouting in nasal voices. One was holding an áṋshbaṋt́i [baṋt́i means a device specially for cutting fish and non-vegetarian stuff], and the other held a muŕojháṋt́á [a worn-out broom]. From their nasal tone I realized that they were not humans, but female ghosts. On listening to them I surmised that they were two sisters-in-law, [the wife of oneʼs husbandʼs brother].

points.body: The younger sister-in-law was saying, “My husbandʼs monthly income is Rs. 3000, while your husbandʼs income is only Rs. 2000. Even so, I have to take my turn and suffer the heat of the kitchen hearth [using wood as fuel] for part of the day. But why should I suffer it? I will no longer run the kitchen. I would like to spend that time either going to the cinema or by enjoying fresh air by climbing a shyáoŕá tree [in traditional folk tales, ghosts like to live in these trees]. Your husband earns less, so you should do the cooking both times.”

points.body: The elder sister-in-law said, “It is said that in a place where there is no tree, even a brinjal plant is considered a tree ( 1 ). (I at once noted down these words in my notebook, realizing that this is the appropriate Bengali for erańd́oapi drumáyate.) You come from a very poor family. You had never seen Rs. 3000 at a time since your birth. On coming here you saw it and it went to your head. From today onwards, donʼt introduce yourself as a female ghost because that will only provoke peopleʼs laughter. Furthermore, it is not true that your husband really earns Rs. 3000 per month. His actual salary is just barely Rs. 1000, and the rest he manages by smuggling bed sheets, towels, medicines and phenyl from the hospital to the black market. Today I will burst the balloon of your Rs. 3000 lie. I shall inform the officers of the Intelligence Department about this pilfering and smuggling (‘Detective’ means ”intelligence“. The word t́ikt́iki [lizard] has come form the word ‘detective’). They will crack down on your scoundrel husband, rope him in and send him to jail.”

points.body: The younger sister-in-law of the female ghost then said, “You can do whatever you like. I shall cut off the tail of the lizard [meaning the detective] with my áṋshbaṋt́i. My darling child is never served fish heads, while your child, who is as ugly as an owl, with the face of a clay stove, eats rui [Labio rohita] fish heads every day. I cannot stand it any longer. Oh God, please do something about it today itself!”

points.body: At this, both of them hurriedly went to climb a nearby palm tree. I said, “You should not both climb the same palm tree, because if you start scuffling up in the tree, you will both fall down and break your bones. You were once humans, and after death you have become female ghosts. But if you die again I cannot imagine what will happen to you! So if you want to have a peaceful rest, then you had better climb separate trees, and relax.”

points.body: Then they climbed up two separate trees. I had some urgent work, so I started hurrying to Pandua station to catch a train. While walking, I heard from afar a film song that the female ghosts were singing in rásabha rágińii [the melodic mode of a donkey] from the top of the palm trees. I had learnt a new expression: in a place where there is no tall tree, even a brinjal plant is considered a tree.

points.body: The inherent weaknesses which harm humans are called ripus [enemies]. And the kind of constraints that attack a human by taking opportunity of these ripus and oppress him like a millstone around his neck, are called pásha. The ripus are six in number: káma [desire], krodha [anger], lobha [avarice], mada [pride or vanity], moha [blind attachment], mátsarya [jealousy]; and the bonds which bind a person on account of the presence of these ripus are called páshas [pásha means bandhanarajju ( 1 ) or bondage]. They are eight in number:

points.body: Thus, hatred, doubt, fear, shyness, censure, vanity of lineage, cultural superiority complex, and egotism are the eight bondages. The biijamantra [acoustic root] of the bondage of hatred is pa. A bond does not necessarily relate to only one ripu; it can involve several. However, the bondages of hatred and fear, in spite of their association with other ripus are mainly related to the ripu of attachment. Suppose somebody is addicted to drinking. The mind moves downward when the attraction is materialistic. The verb pat [patati] is used for the downward motion. The addiction leads to oneʼs fall. And when the motion is upward it is called anurakti and the ultimate form of anurakti is called bhakti [devotion]. This is the reason why the verb in Sanskrit for such movement is urdhva gam (urdhvagacchati). One who has the weakness of an addiction to drinking becomes easily bound by hatred and fear. Not only addiction to drinking, any kind of attachment makes one both detestable to others and afraid of others. One runs after a delusion without any rhyme or reason. This idea of attachment brings a story to my mind.

points.body: An acquaintance of mine lived in Mominpur – I canʼt exactly recollect his name, possibly it was Mańd́ámohon Mukhujje. Some people called Mandamohan an extremely niggardly miser, some said he was a myopic miser, some said he was so closefisted that even water would not pass through his fingers. Some said that if he had to spend even one pice, he would feel as if he had broken a rib; some said that he was “one pice father, mother” [for him, to part with even a single pice is like to give up his father or mother], some said he was “one pice pyáṋjphulurii [onion vegetable chop]”, some humourously called him pyáṋj-payjár. Modern boys called him “upurhasta no-not-never” [he who never extends his hand in a giving gesture, one who never gives anything]. He immensely enjoyed all these appellations.

summary: That year there was an overproduction of brinjal. The farmers in a country where there is no scientific economic structure become practically ruined when there
points.body: That year there was an overproduction of brinjal. The farmers in a country where there is no scientific economic structure become practically ruined when there is an over production. That year, the farmers of Bengal were practically ruined on account of the over production of brinjal. Once, I went to the village of Bego under the Haringhata Police Station in Nadia District and there I saw that the farmers where cutting brinjal into pieces and, after adding some salt, giving them to the cows. As soon as a cow which was about to eat it noticed that it was brinjal, it turned its face away and said humbá humbá. As it tried to take its food from another part of the pot, it saw brinjal there also and again it refused to eat. The farmers realized that if the cows stopped eating fodder they would not yield any milk, so they stopped serving brinjal to the cows.

points.body: The farmers of Ramnagar of Birbhum District were traditional cultivators of brinjal. On going there I heard that they had stopped plucking the brinjal from the plants. They told me, “Sir, let the brinjal rot on the plants. It will be more useful as compost.” I could not go to Panjipara for lack of time, so I cannot say what happened to the famous brinjal of that place. In those days, articles were sold in the wholesale market in our town in pasurii. Five seers made one pasurii and eight pasuriis made one mund. But there was no uniform measure of seer in all the districts. A standard seer meant eighty tolás [1 tola is 11.664 grams, so a standard seer would be 933.12 grams]. But in our Monghyr District a seer was eighty four tolas. Again, in the neighbouring district of Bhagalpur, it varied from a hundred, a hundred and one, and a hundred and three tolás in different places. In some places, a seer was even a hundred and five tolás.

points.body: A seer made of sixty tolás was called káṋci account [rough calculation]. Anyway that year, on account of the over production of brinjal, brinjal was aplenty in our town. In Mańd́ámohanʼs house the regular menu for three months at a stretch was rice and burnt brinjal. The women of the locality used to ask Mońd́ámohanʼs wife, Shrimatii Mithyámayii Devii [mithyá means “lies”], “Well, mother of Markat (The name of Mańd́ámohanʼs son was Markat́mohan [markat́ means “monkey”] Mukhujje. He used to sell lottery tickets and do private tuition. He would have his tiffin in the homes of his students, but preferred to chew harimat́ar ( 2 ) on holidays, that is, he preferred not to eat anything) . She used to answer, “Today, from early dawn until twelve noon, I worked continuously in the kitchen, so I have aches in my neck and back.”

points.body: People asked her, “What did you spend such a long time cooking?” She said, “ First I prepared a dish of brinjal and margosa leaves; then I prepared a dry dish of brinjal stalks, then grilled brinjal, then brinjal balls, then brinjal broth with pasted ginger, a hot dish of brinjal with pasted mustard seed, and finally a sweet dish made of brinjal seeds with sugarcane molasses. I also wanted to prepare a dish of brinjal with paddy seeds, but that could not be done because the fire in the oven became low by then. I donʼt allow burnt brinjal anywhere near my kitchen (I never ever cook burnt brinjal. That is only for poor people).”

points.body: Once, in our locality, preparations for Kali Puja [worship of the goddess Káli] were being made with great pomp and show. Some boys were busy with theatre rehearsals. Some of them felt an acute shortage of money. Earlier, they used to manage some money from the shopping expenses of the family, but now, on account of growing expenses, their father started doing the shopping, himself. To combat the resultant lack of commission, some of the overenthusiastic boys started going around collecting subscriptions. People paid subscriptions according to their capacity. When Mańd́ámahon was asked to pay a subscription, he was visibly shocked. He said, “Oh God, you are talking about Kali! She is a great, belligerent lady, and we are devout Vaeśńavas. We canʼt worship Kali, it is forbidden by our ancestors.”

points.body: The boys thought, “Maybe there is a restriction.” And so they left. The next day all the people of the locality were invited to sit in rows and eat the maháprasáda, the food that had been offered to the goddess Kali. It was noticed that the person who sat first in the front row was none other than Shri Mańd́ámohon Mukhujje.

points.body: A story which is historically famous comes to my mind. The name of the village was Kuŕiye Kháoyá [eating leftovers]. Mr. Kipt́ekaiṋjus Kar [Kipt́e means “an extremely miserly person”] was a famous man of that place. Kipt́ekaiṋjus used to earn a lot of money in various legal and illegal ways. It dawned on him that if he wanted to suddenly become rich, it would be necessary to get a boon from Lord Shiva. To please other gods, it is necessary to perform a long and difficult penance. But Shiva is Bholanath [one who easily forgets peopleʼs misdeeds] and Ashutośa [One who is easily satisfied]. He becomes happy even if one offers him one ákanda flower [Calotropis gigantea] and a few leaves of the bel [Aegle marmelos] tree. So he decided to worship him.

points.body: Kipt́ekaiṋjus started moving on and on with interminable speed. He did not look at the trees because he had not come to do research on plants. He did not take note of the way the birds and animals lived because he had no time to think about them. Was he thinking of Lord Shiva? No, certainly not. Lord Shiva was now closed out of his mind. Was he thinking of Kuber? No, not him, either. He was thinking of Kuberʼs wealth.

points.body: Kipt́ekaiṋjus travelled on. He was not afraid of tigers, nor of snakes, nor of crocodiles emerging from the water. He was lost in thoughts of wealth; this strong attachment blurred his vision. He had no time to ponder what others would say or think. He walked on and on, through his extreme greed for money. Suddenly, something came into view and Kipt́ekaiṋjus stopped. He was not able to believe his eyes. In front of him there was a hill of cowries [kaŕi ( 2 )], on his right there was a mountain of cowries, on the left there was a hillock of cowries and at the back a mound of cowries. He declared victory. But whose victory? Not the victory of Shiva, nor the victory of Kuber. It was the victory of cowries.

points.body: In the next moment he thought, “But what is the value of a cowrie?” He had just six pockets, four on his coat and two in his trousers. Even if he filled all six pockets with cowries, they wouldnʼt be of much value.

points.body: Kipt́ekaiṋjus rejected the cowries and moved on. After walking some distance, he saw another hill in front of him. It was a hill of copper [táṋbá ( 3 ) ] coins. Kiptekainjus thought that although copper coins are much more valuable than cowries, even then, six pocketfuls of copper coins would not make him really a rich man. So he crossed the copper hill and moved on.

points.body: Kipt́ekaiṋjus felt that to fill his six pockets with silver coins involved three problems. First, the total value of the silver coins was not so much. Secondly, he would not be able to walk fast on account of the weight of the silver coins. Thirdly, the coins would make a clanking sound and this would give the impression to thieves and dacoits that he had a lot of money.

points.body: In those days, there was no Rs.1 currency note. In the British period, the use of cowries was banned. Coins made of copper, bronze, or silver were mostly in use. (Gold coins with alloy, which are called sovereigns in English and gini in Bengali, from which we have the word ginisońá, were also used, though they were scarce.) That is why the shopkeepers, when going home from their shops, used to put their coins in a bundle and tightly tie them up so that they did not make any noise. The bundle of even a small merchant usually contained a large number of coins.

points.body: While talking about the merchantsʼ bundles, I remember a story of those days. Once, a guru went on a round of the houses of his disciples to collect money. It was wintertime, just after harvesting, the most appropriate time for collecting money. In honour of the guruʼs visit, the disciples gave him a warm reception and delicious treats. At this time, a particular disciple had a lot of money. At night, he asked his guru, “Master, itʼs winter now. Will you use a blanket or a quilt at night? I have both ready for you.” The guru thought, “Let me pretend to be a god-man this time.”

points.body: Once upon a time, a few dead crows were lying scattered about the hermitage of a fakir [a Muslim ascetic]. People asked him, “Fakir Saheb, why did so many forest crows die in the storm?” The Fakir replied, “The crows used to disturb me a lot. Yesterday evening I strongly warned them. I said to them, ‘f you donʼt behave properly I will finish you all offʼ. Just see, before a single night had passed, they all were struck dead by the storm. Had they followed my instruction and learnt to cuckoo instead of cawing, they would not have suffered such a fate.”

Thus, there is a Bengali proverb – jhaŕe kák mare phakirer kyáramatii báŕe [The crows die in a storm and the fakir gets the credit]. The guru thought, “Let me also show my charisma in the house of this disciple of mine.”

points.body: After dinner, the guru went to his room. The disciple was a very good person. He kept sitting at the door with a blanket wrapped around him, so that if his guru should feel cold, he could immediately give him a quilt or a blanket. He saw, through a chink in the door, that in the first part of the night his guru was lying straight, with his hands and legs outstretched. He said to himself, “In the first part of the night my master is an incarnation of a d́heṋki [a kind of husking pedal operated in a seesaw manner]. In the second part of the night, the guru started feeling cold and he drew up his knees. The disciple outside broke into a song, “In the second part of the night my master is a stringed bow.” During the third part of the night it became colder, and the body of the guru also shrank in cold. The disciple sang, “In the third part of the night my master is curled up like a dog”. In the fourth part of the night, as it became very cold, the body of the guru looked almost like a circle. On seeing this, the disciple sang, “In the fourth part of the night, my master is a merchantʼs bundle.” However, we return to the point that Kipt́ekaiṋjus did not want to move around with a merchantʼs bundle.

points.body: He moved forward. Kipt́ekaiṋjus moved on and on for days and months. He passed many sleepless nights and was drenched many times by rain, but Kipt́ekaiṋjus did not care about any of this. His sole aim was to collect wealth, and his mind kept on whispering, “I am hungry, I am hungry.”

points.body: On seeing the hill of gold, Kipt́ekaiṋjus was simply dazzled. He thought, “Oh God, at last my lifelong wish of this life and many previous lives is finally fulfilled. Today I am the richest person, but how shall I carry all this wealth home? Where shall I keep it? I shall further increase my wealth through interest accrued on it. Until now, I used to have only muŕi [puffed rice] with oil, salt and green chilli for my breakfast. From now on, I shall leave out the chillies and eat only dry muŕi to reduce my expenditure. I must increase my income, but the final problem is how to carry this wealth home? This hill of gold cannot be stuffed into my six pockets.”

After going some distance he saw that there was a hill of precious stones [mańi] – gems, pearls and jewels. He could easily buy a hill of gold with a handful of those gems and jewels.

points.body: He thought, “Since I have come this far, let me move a little farther on and see if I can get something more valuable.” He kept on running, with tired limbs and almost out of breath. He started sweating all over and even then he went on running and running. Was there no end to this running?

points.body: After covering some distance, he saw that a brahmadatyi [brahmadaetya] [a man-eating ghost of a Brahman] was standing in the middle of the road, and a huge wheel with very sharp blades was rotating on his head. His head was cut open by the wheel so that the soft grey matter of his brain was coming out and he was bleeding profusely. The brahmadaitya was crying at the top of his lungs: “Oh, I am undone. Alas, I am undone, I am dying, please save me, I donʼt want money, I donʼt want wealth, I only want peace, I want that peace which is the greatest wealth of life!” The drops of blood spilling out of the brahmadaityaʼs head were scattering about on all sides, and from every drop of blood was born an extremely greedy person. These people, quarreling and fighting amongst themselves, grovelled in the dust until they died. The last particle of their existence was lost in the bottomless abyss of darkness.

summary: Kipt́ekaiṋjus asked the brahmadaitya, “My dear brother, why is that rotating wheel on your head? How come cakraḿ bhramati mastake [that wheel is rotating on y
points.body: Kipt́ekaiṋjus asked the brahmadaitya, “My dear brother, why is that rotating wheel on your head? How come cakraḿ bhramati mastake [that wheel is rotating on your head] endlessly?” As soon as Kipt́ekaiṋjus uttered these words, the wheel left the brahmadaityaʼs head, landed on his own head and started rotating very fast. Kiptekainjus cried out in excruciating agony, “I donʼt want wealth, I have been going on the wrong path. I donʼt want Kuberʼs wealth through Shivaʼs recommendation. I want peace, the profound peace that is ensconced in Shiva. Please save me, whoever is around, please save me, I am undone, I am dying! Is there nobody to save me? I want only Shiva, Shiva smeared with ashes.”

summary: The brahmadaitya said, “I was also extremely greedy and a victim of attachment, like you. I also arrived here just as you did. On reaching here I saw that a whe
points.body: The brahmadaitya said, “I was also extremely greedy and a victim of attachment, like you. I also arrived here just as you did. On reaching here I saw that a wheel was rotating on the head of a brahmapisháca. I also asked him, ”Well, brother, why is a wheel rotating on your head?“ The arrangement, as decided by Lord Shiva, is that this is the final outcome of attachment: Cakraḿ bhramati mastake. If some other person, as greedy as you, comes and asks you, 'My dear brother, why is that wheel rotating on your head?ʼ the wheel will immediately move onto his head, and you will be relieved from its oppression. Well, brother, I am off. I donʼt know how long I was in the condition of cakraḿ bhrumarti mastake. I must return now.”

points.body: An enlightened human, resplendent with the brilliance of wisdom, was never so since the moment of his or her birth. Enlightenment and rationality free from dogmatic ideas come step by step at a certain stage of the rhythmic movement of the development of human consciousness through various impediments and constraints. I cannot say that the humans of today have become completely free from dogmas. In fact, the humans of today are yet to become free from superstitions. This is the reason why there are so many clashes, murders, quarrels, squabbles and misunderstandings among humans. Those who give the excuse of misunderstanding usually deliberately misunderstand or pretend to misunderstand in order to fulfill their own interests. Yet, the wisdom of the humans of earlier times must certainly have been less profound than that of the humans of today. Their lives were based on blind attachment to dogmas. Those superstitions of theirs, continuing for such a long time, have done a great injury to a large part of society, making it suffer the cataclysmic crisis of decadence. Those people who tried to control this decadence either died out, or somehow survived and trudged on with broken knees. The idea of the yakśa was one such superstition born out of dogmatic beliefs.

points.body: A yakśa [was considered to be] an assistant of Kuber [the god of wealth], so it would never allow wealth to go to waste. On the strength of this belief, people would build a small room under the earth, in which to keep their wealth. They would seat a young, dark-skinned boy there, in front of a lighted lamp, and perform some occult rites (this type of negative occult ritual is called pha). Then, on coming back above ground, they would cover the roof of that room with earth, camouflaging it with the adjoining land so that nobody would suspect anything from outside. After sometime, the flame of the lamp would go out, and simultaneously, the lamp of that innocent boyʼs life would also be extinguished. He would fall into an eternal slumber in the abyss of darkness.

points.body: People believed that the boy would turn into a yakśa and that he would guard the wealth. They thought that he would be freed only after he had handed over the entire wealth to the rightful owner at the appropriate time. In Bengali, this type of wealth was called yakher dhan in common speech. In Bihar, the places which were known to have such wealth were called brhamasthán [the seat of Brahma]. Even today, one can find such brahmastháns under a huge banyan tree or a pipul tree [Ficus religiosa] outside the villages. Nobody likes to go to such places – in fact, people are afraid to go to such places after sunset.

points.body: Not only those innocent boys but also young, innocent dark-skinned girls were subjected to the atrocities of the superstitious process of making a yakśa. A wealthy man would dig a huge tank and keep his wealth at the bottom of it. A young, dark-skinned girl would have her hands and legs tied, and would be drowned in that tank, while occult rituals were performed (needless to say, this was also called pha). The moment the dead body of the girl surfaced, it was presumed that the dead girl had turned into a yakśińii [a female yakśa]. It was believed that when the rightful owner of that wealth would come to that tank in future, the yakśińii would hand over the wealth to him, and she would then become free. Such a yakśińii used to be called yakhe buŕii in the Bengali vernacular of that time. A tank where such macabre rituals were performed was called yakher pukur [a yakśaʼs tank] or tálpukur [a tank with palm trees]. Some people think that if the water in a tank is deep (tál is a measure of water, such as báṋo), then that tank is called a tálpukur. This is not wholly true. Palm trees were planted around a tank just to mislead people. There is a prevalent notion that in the event of a sudden need of a large number of utensils on account of some feast or yajiṋa [an elaborate worship], if a girl goes to that tank, stands in the neck-deep water and prays to the yakhe buŕii, then the following morning, the yakhe buŕii will supply the utensils and leave them on the bank of the tank. After the ceremonial function is over it is necessary to return the utensils after washing them clean, and leaving them on the bank of the tank. It is believed that if some greedy person steals those utensils, the yakhe buŕii will catch hold of their legs and drag them down to hell when they come to the tank again in future.

points.body: While talking about yakher dhan and yakhe buŕii, I remember Bhuṋŕobhombal Bhar. He lived in Bhoṋdaŕpur, near Bhadreshvar. For breakfast he used to buy one pice worth of pyáṋj phulurii [a kind of vegetable chop made of powdered pigeon-peas and onions] in the morning, and would eat this four times a day for refreshment. Bhuṋŕobhombal had a huge property, a huge collection of dazzling gems and jewels, such as diamonds, sapphires and many other precious stones. Bhuṋŕobhombal worried what would happen if his descendents squandered his enormous wealth. What would happen if they wasted all his things? In that case he would not find peace even after death.

points.body: Báburám Bhar was his only son. You know the functions of five generations in regard to wealth. The first generation only buys property and collects wealth. So it may be called Kenárám [the buying generation]. The second generation enjoys the property, spends it in luxury and swaggers about in aristocratic style. It may be called Báburám [the luxurious generation]. The third generation maintains the same luxurious habits by selling the property. It may be called Becárám [the selling generation]. During the selling generation, the property practically becomes completely exhausted, and as a result the next generation spends its days in great hardship. So it may be called Dukhiirám [the suffering generation]. After Duhkhiirám, there is practically no property left, so the fifth generation takes to begging for a living. This may be called Bhikhurám [the begging generation]. So our Bhuṋŕobhombal was Kenárám and his only son was Báburám.

points.body: For his lunch and dinner, Bhuṋŕobhombal used to have newly harvested aush rice [rice made from paddy which ripens in the rainy season or autumn] with rice water. The new aush rice takes time to digest, so a little quantity fills the stomach. People used to ask him, “Why donʼt you strain the water from the rice?” He used to reply, “Doctors say that the water contains vitamins.” He used to eat burnt brinjals with boiled rice, because compared to fried brinjal, burnt brinjal needs very little oil, so little, in fact, that it can be burnt even without using any oil. He used to collect jujubes that had fallen from the tree, prepare a sour curry with them and eat it. When jujubes were not available he used to buy a few hog plums or tamarind and prepare a sour sauce, and felt very unhappy that he had to incur an additional expenditure. He felt uneasy during the day and could not sleep at night. After the expulsion of his son his expenditure was considerably reduced.

points.body: One day, he thought, “Who knows into whose extravagant hands my huge property will fall after my death?” He decided to bury his wealth under the ground and hand it over to a yakh [yakśa]. He thought that the yakh would hand over that wealth to the rightful heir or he would take it back from the yakh when he was reborn as a human being in his next birth. He did not look for a mason to construct the underground room in which to keep the wealth meant for the yakh. There were two reasons for this. The first and foremost reason was that the mason in that case would come to know about the hidden wealth. And the second reason was that it had often happened that cruel people had murdered the mason after their underground room had been constructed, so that the secret would not leak out. Once these crimes became public knowledge, masons were not willing to build underground rooms for hiding wealth. So Bhuṋŕobhombal started building the room himself with various necessary implements and building materials. It is not an easy job to make a room underground.

points.body: After some time, the room was finished. Bhuṋŕobhombal also took lessons from a negative occultist in the rituals to be performed for making a yakśa. However, it was difficult to find a young, dark-skinned boy. He avidly waited, like the crow of a sacred place, for a such a boy to come in the direction of his house, by chance. Even the beggar boys never came near his house because he never gave any alms. On the contrary, instead of getting alms they got a beating. One day, he saw that a dark-skinned boy of about five years old was passing by his house. He was wearing silver bangles. In Bengal, in those days, both men and women used to wear bangles. Both the children of well-to-do families as well as those of ordinary families used to wear golden bangles, while the poor ones used to wear bangles made of silver or bell metal. On seeing the boyʼs silver bangles, Bhuṋŕobhombal understood that the boy belonged to a poor family. He then tempted the boy with a treat of sweets and brought him within the compound of his house. Then he led him to the underground room, and lighting a lamp before him, started performing the occult rituals. We have already said that such a ritual is pha. The lamp was burning, flickering, and intermittently blazing up rather tremulously. The boy became afraid and wanted to go away. He started imploring and crying to be let go. But the impervious heart of Bhuṋŕobhombal did not melt. He left the boy there, and covered the room by spreading earth over it. Certainly, the lamp became extinguished after sometime, and the lamp of that boyʼs life was also extinguished forever. Bhuṋŕobhombal, full of joy, went back to his house. He was happy that at last a solution had been found for preserving his huge property. Today, fully satisfied, he would eat stale rice with a curry made of potato skins, then have a deep sleep.

As he was lying down he heard the dark-skinned boy mumbling into his right ear, “Please let me go, let me go home.” As it became unbearable, he plugged his right ear. But then he started hearing the boy mumbling into his left ear, “Please let me go, my mother will cry for me.” He plugged both his ears. Then he started seeing a nightmare in front of his eyes. He saw that the little boy was crying, pleading, “I am certainly not a bad boy. Then why are you killing me? Donʼt you know that my father will go about looking for me everywhere?”
